title: Survey on Monocular Metric Depth Estimation
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant – the paper is a dedicated survey of Monocular Metric Depth Estimation (MMDE) covering the period up to 2025, discusses datasets, methodological trends (adaptive binning, transformer designs, zero‑shot/generalization), key models (Zoedepth, Depth Anything, UniDepth, PatchFusion, DMD, Marigold, GeoWizard), and outlines current limitations and open challenges, directly matching the requested 2023‑2025 scope.
key_findings: MMDE has shifted from geometry‑based pipelines to deep models that predict absolute depth, enabling metric‑scale 3D perception for SLAM, navigation, and view synthesis.
Adaptive‑binning techniques (AdaBins, LocalBins, BinsFormer) and transformer‑based architectures markedly improve depth accuracy and scale consistency.
Zero‑shot/generalizable models such as ZoeDepth, UniDepth and Depth Anything demonstrate strong cross‑domain performance by leveraging massive semi‑supervised data (e.g., 62 M self‑annotated images).
Patch‑based inference (PatchFusion, PatchRefiner) helps preserve fine‑grained boundaries but incurs higher computational cost.
Generative diffusion approaches (Marigold, GeoWizard, DMD) can recover high‑frequency details and handle challenging materials, yet remain slower and often produce relative rather than metric depth.
Hybrid sensor prompting (sparse LiDAR cues) offers a practical route to boost metric accuracy while keeping a vision‑centric pipeline.
limitations: Generalization to unseen domains still suffers from geometric blurring and loss of fine detail, especially in high‑resolution or outdoor scenes.
Patch‑based methods improve detail but scale poorly with image size, limiting real‑time deployment.
Diffusion‑based MMDE provides superior fidelity but requires multi‑step inference, leading to latency and higher memory usage.
Benchmarking is hindered by inconsistent datasets, training protocols, and a lack of standardized evaluation for metric depth.
Many state‑of‑the‑art models depend on large‑scale annotated or pseudo‑labeled data, raising concerns about data bias and robustness.
evidence_snippets: “Monocular Metric Depth Estimation (MMDE) overcomes this challenge by producing depth maps with absolute scale… This survey reviews the evolution of MMDE, from geometry‑based methods to state‑of‑the‑art deep models…” (Abstract)

summary: The survey provides a comprehensive overview of Monocular Metric Depth Estimation (MMDE) up to 2025, tracing its evolution from geometry‑based pipelines to deep learning models that produce absolute‑scale depth maps. It highlights methodological breakthroughs such as adaptive binning (AdaBins, LocalBins, BinsFormer), transformer‑based encoders, and large‑scale semi‑supervised training (Depth Anything, ZoeDepth, UniDepth) that enable strong zero‑shot generalization across indoor and outdoor domains. Patch‑based refinements improve boundary preservation but increase latency, while diffusion generative models (Marigold, GeoWizard, DMD) offer high‑frequency detail at the cost of computational efficiency. The paper identifies persistent challenges: domain generalization, fine‑detail loss, inference speed, and the lack of standardized benchmarks. Future directions emphasize efficient architectures, hybrid sensor prompting, and better loss designs to achieve universally accurate, fast, and metric‑consistent depth estimation.

title: Deep Learning-based Depth Estimation Methods from Monocular Image and Videos: A Comprehensive Survey
source: Full text of the paper (provided in chunks)
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant. The paper surveys >160 deep learning based monocular depth estimation works from 2012‑2024, presents a taxonomy (input/output modalities, network architectures, supervision levels, datasets, domain adaptation), discusses challenges, pipelines, loss functions, and future directions, directly addressing the state‑of‑the‑art 2023‑2025 landscape.
key_findings: Monocular depth estimation methods are classified by input (single image or video), output (dense/sparse, absolute/relative), architecture (CNN, ViT, RNN, GAN, hybrid), and supervision (3‑D supervised, self‑supervised, semi‑/weakly‑supervised, online learning).
Self‑supervised methods dominate recent research, using photometric reprojection losses with stereo or video cues, but suffer from occlusions, dynamic objects, and texture‑less regions.
Vision‑Transformer‑based backbones and CNN‑ViT hybrids improve generalization by capturing long‑range dependencies, yet remain computationally expensive.
Domain adaptation techniques (fine‑tuning, style‑transfer GANs) are essential for day‑night, indoor‑outdoor, and synthetic‑real transfers.
Key limitations include poor depth for thin/distant objects, reflective/transparent materials, reliance on accurate camera poses, and lack of explainability.
limitations: Self‑supervised approaches struggle with moving objects, occlusions, and repetitive textures, often requiring masking strategies that reduce usable data.
Transformer‑based models have high memory/computation cost, limiting real‑time deployment on embedded devices.
Most surveys (including this one) focus on RGB‑D datasets; synthetic datasets lack realistic lighting and material properties, hindering transferability.
Current methods rarely address extreme viewpoints (aerial, fisheye, worm’s‑eye) or sub‑pixel accuracy required in medical/industrial applications.
evidence_snippets: “We present a taxonomy of existing methods that consolidate their input and output modalities, network architectures, and supervision modes.”
“Self‑supervised monocular depth estimation methods tackle the challenge of not having enough ground‑truth 3D data for training… using a photometric similarity loss function…”
“Vision Transformers represent an image as a series of patches… They are known to be a better solution than the CNNs as they overcome the limited receptive field issue.”
“Domain adaptation is crucial… GAN‑based style transfer methods… adapt synthetic data to real‑world domains.”
“Inaccurate results for thin, small, and distant objects… Estimating depth for such objects is challenging.”
summary: The survey provides a comprehensive, taxonomy‑driven overview of deep learning‑based monocular depth estimation up to 2024, covering over 160 papers and detailing input/output formats, network designs, supervision strategies, datasets, and domain adaptation methods. It highlights the prominence of self‑supervised learning with photometric reprojection losses, the rise of Vision Transformers and hybrid CNN‑ViT architectures for better global context, and the importance of domain adaptation to bridge synthetic‑real gaps. Persistent challenges include handling dynamic scenes, occlusions, thin or reflective objects, and the computational burden of transformer models, limiting real‑time deployment. The paper also identifies under‑explored areas such as extreme viewpoints, sub‑pixel accuracy for medical use, and model interpretability, outlining directions for future research.
